The conflict arises from mutually exclusive claims about transferability and real-world impact within the same scope and time window.

The cited evidence collectively yields a cautious conclusion: there is credible evidence that brain training can produce measurable gains on the trained tasks, but high-quality studies and consensus statements indicate these gains typically do not generalize to broader cognitive function or everyday life. The evidence divides into two camps. Multiple rigorous studies and consensus statements report that while participants can improve performance on the specific tasks they train, these benefits do not transfer to untrained cognitive abilities or everyday decision-making, arguing against broad cognitive improvement from commercial brain training [d3,d6,d9,d10,d11]. In contrast, other high-credibility sources acknowledge some benefits in trained skills or related domains (e.g., ACTIVE trial improvements, enhanced brain connectivity, or small short-term effects), but they do not demonstrate durable, generalizable gains across cognition [d1,d2,d4,d7]. Because the strongest studies find no transfer beyond trained tasks and authoritative reviews caution that commercial brain games lack evidence for lasting, general cognitive benefits, the most defensible stance is that Brain Training does not reliably improve general cognitive function beyond practice effects on the trained tasks [d3,d6,d7,d9,d10,d11].
